1.goal: To open the lesson on a piece of news she heard, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
run: Ask whether she did the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she reads an article that mixes facts and forecasts and tells a CEO what is certain and what is not.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you read a news article where some things have happened and some are only forecasts. Then you brief someone who has not read it.”
If she answers in general terms: “Who told you, and how did you check whether it was true?”
1.expected: One piece of news someone repeated to her this week and why she was not sure about it, in two or three sentences. A complete answer looks like “A colleague said the dollar was going to reach six reais, but it was only one analyst’s opinion.” — the news, who said it, and why it was not certain. Any news she brings is right here.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, name two areas and let her pick one: something about prices or the economy, or something about her company or her sector.
1.challenge: Ask what she would need to see before repeating that news in a meeting.
1.monitoring: Whether she separates what happened from what someone said will happen, and how she says any number.
1.evidence: The news she brought, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has named one piece of news and who said it.

2.goal: To establish who is asking, what the CEO needs, and what she should leave the conversation with.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “The CEO needs to know what the article really reports, and what is only planned, expected or possible, so that a forecast is not repeated as a fact.” Both parts are in the last two lines of the brief; the content of the article is not named here.
2.support: If she answers with what the article might say, point at “What you want by the end” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask what the CEO’s question, “Is this going to happen to us?”, can and cannot be answered with one article.
2.monitoring: Whether she states the task from the brief or starts guessing the content.
2.evidence: Whether she can say the task in one sentence without rereading.
2.transition: Move on when she has said, in one sentence, what the CEO needs.

3.goal: To have her commit to three guesses before she reads, so the reading has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Nothing is confirmed or corrected here.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one answer on each and leave them unconfirmed: the article on the next screen settles them.
Note her three answers where she can see them.
exact: Before moving on: “Those are your guesses. Now we read and see.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: the three questions are open. For your reference, the article will show ships arriving in groups and longer shifts at a warehouse, a hiring plan, a figure about people leaving that comes from a union, and forecasts from the carriers, an analyst and a consultancy.
3.support: If she answers about logistics in general, ask her to answer as if it were a distribution center she knows.
3.challenge: Ask which of her three guesses she would bet on, and why.
3.monitoring: Whether she draws on her own experience in logistics HR.
3.evidence: Her three guesses, kept for screen 4.
3.transition: Move on when all three questions have an answer, right or wrong.

4.goal: To read the article once for the story: what has already happened, and what has not happened yet.
run: Give her about three minutes for the article.
Ask the question on screen.
Then ask which of her guesses from screen 3 the article confirms.
4.expected: Already happened: a shipping route closed, the detour adds nine to twelve days, and Norvale moved its largest site to 12-hour shifts on arrival days in May. Not yet: the hiring of up to 300 temporary workers, the reopening of the route, and any decision about the Campinas site, on which the company “declined to comment.”
4.support: If she lists numbers, ask her to say the story first without any number.
4.challenge: Ask which sentence in the article a CEO would most likely repeat wrongly.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for the whole or stops on the figures.
4.evidence: How long she takes, and whether she reads the article once or goes back while answering.
4.transition: Move on when she has said what has happened and at least two things that have not.

5.goal: To attribute each of six statements to the source in the article that gives it, going back to the line instead of answering from memory.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Let her place all six on her own and press Check when she has finished. The button checks the whole activity at once.
Then go through the six out loud. On each, ask her to open the article with the button on screen and read the line that decides it.
Spend the time that is left on the Campinas site and on the union figure.
exact: On each statement: “Which line says that? Read it to me.”
On the Campinas site: “The article mentions Campinas. Does anyone say it is closing?”
5.expected: The carriers: “The detour adds nine to twelve days to each trip.” (“…, according to two of the largest carriers.”) · “The route will reopen by the end of the year.” (“The carriers expect…”). The company: “Norvale will hire up to 300 temporary workers before November.” (“The company says it will hire…”). A union representative: “At least 60 people have left the largest site since April.” — and Norvale “has not confirmed that figure.” The consultancy: “Between 800 and 1,200 warehouse jobs could move to temporary contracts.” Nobody in the article: “Norvale is closing its Campinas site.” — the article only says that “Norvale declined to comment on its plans for its Campinas site.”
5.support: If she answers from memory, open the article and ask her to find the line before she chooses.
5.challenge: Ask which of the six a CEO would most likely repeat wrongly in a meeting.
5.monitoring: Whether she goes back to the article. Campinas is where a rumor and a real line meet; if she places it with the company, ask what the company actually said.
5.evidence: Whether she returned to the article, and what she did with Campinas and with the union figure.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed and Campinas has been discussed.

6.goal: To have her notice that small words around the information tell the reader whether it is already happening, planned or expected, or only possible.
6.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S.
run: Let her classify the six phrases and press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each, ask her to find it in the article and read the whole sentence.
Then ask her what happens to a sentence if the word that marks it is taken out.
exact: After the check: “Take out ‘could’ and ‘if the detour lasts into next year’. What does the CEO hear now?”
6.expected: It is already happening: “adds nine to twelve days to each trip” · “moved its largest site to 12-hour shifts”. It is planned or expected: “will hire up to 300 temporary workers” · “expect the route to reopen”. It could happen: “could move to temporary contracts” · “could easily be March”. Without “could” and “if”, the sentence says that 800 to 1,200 jobs are moving to temporary contracts — something nobody in the article says.
6.support: On each phrase, ask: has it happened, has someone planned or predicted it, or is it only possible?
6.challenge: Ask for one more phrase in the article that shows how sure the information is. “Has not confirmed” is one; “declined to comment” is another.
6.monitoring: Whether she sees the job of each phrase in context. She reads fast and may classify by the verb alone.
6.evidence: Which of the six she placed elsewhere, if any.
6.transition: Move on when the six are sorted and she has said what changes without the words.

7.goal: To have her find that “up to 300” and “at least 300” put the same number at opposite ends, and to see how the article’s other numbers work.
run: Read the question and the three sentences with her.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open the difference and read it with her. Then ask her to say the union figure or the consultancy estimate in one sentence of her own.
exact: If she does not see it: “With ‘at least 300’, could the company hire 200?”
Asking for her own sentence: “Tell me how many people have left, in a way the CEO cannot misread.”
7.expected: “Norvale will hire at least 300 temporary workers.” is the different one: 300 becomes the lowest number, and the listener imagines 300 or more. “Up to 300” and “as many as 300” both make 300 the highest number. From the reveal: “at least 60” makes 60 the lowest figure, and “between 800 and 1,200” is a range where both ends are said.
7.support: Draw a line from 0 to 500 where she can see it and ask her where 300 sits in each sentence.
7.challenge: Ask what “nearly 300” and “more than 300” would mean, and which one the article supports.
7.monitoring: Whether she finds the difference before the reveal, and whether her own sentence keeps “at least” with the union figure.
7.evidence: Her own sentence with the number, word for word.
7.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has said one sentence of her own.

8.goal: To say the facts, the plan and the forecasts of the article with who says them, before the briefing.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one sentence at a time.
run: Play the five sentences once, and ask her to say each one after it.
Then ask for three pieces of information a CEO would ask about first, one at a time, each with who says it and how sure it is.
When the source or the marker is missing, or a number changes meaning, ask her to say the sentence again.
Open the model briefing after she has said her three pieces of information, and ask where the sources and the markers are in it.
exact: Asking for the first one: “The temporary workers. Tell me, and say who says it.”
Rebuilding a number that lost its marker: “Three hundred exactly? Say it the way the company said it.”
8.expected: Three sentences of this kind, each with the source and the marker: “The company says it will hire up to three hundred temporary workers before November.”, “A union representative says at least sixty people have left since April, but the company has not confirmed it.” and “A consultancy estimates that between eight hundred and one thousand two hundred jobs could move to temporary contracts.” Any form that keeps the source, the marker and the meaning of the number is correct, including forms not on the screen.
8.support: If a number stalls, say its first half and let her finish it.
8.challenge: Ask for the reopening of the route in one sentence that makes clear it is a forecast, and that someone disagrees.
8.monitoring: Which markers she keeps and which she drops; where the source lands.
8.evidence: The numbers that lost or changed their marker, if any.
8.transition: Move on when three pieces of information have been said with their sources.

9.goal: To brief the person she chose on the article, with what has happened, what is planned or expected and what is only possible, each with who says it, and her own reading marked as hers, with the sentence starters closed.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are the person from the option she chose; she briefs you.
run: Read the two options and the list on screen with her, and let her choose.
Let her run until she has given at least two pieces of information. Then interrupt once, with the question for her option, and let her go back to where she was.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, let her look, and close them again.
Leave corrections for screen 11. Write down one sentence with a number, as she said it.
exact: Interruption, option A (CEO): “Sorry — so they are hiring 300 people?”
Interruption, option B (operations director): “Wait. I heard Norvale is closing Campinas. Is that in the article?”
9.expected: Five things in one turn, in the order of the list: what the article is about; what has already happened (the detour, the 12-hour shifts), what is planned or expected (up to 300 temporary workers, the reopening) and what is only possible (the 800 to 1,200 jobs), each with who says it; the numbers with their markers; an answer to the interruption (A: up to 300 — it could be fewer, and the company has not said for how long; B: no — the company declined to comment on Campinas, and nobody in the article says it is closing); and what she would watch in the next weeks, marked as her reading.
9.support: If she stops, point at the next item on the list before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Ask which piece of information she would check before repeating it in a meeting, and why.
9.monitoring: Sources in the sentence, markers kept, numbers with their meaning — and what she does in the first seconds after the interruption.
9.evidence: One sentence of the briefing with a number, written word for word. It goes into the boards on screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has covered the three kinds of information and said what she would watch.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the briefing: answer two questions, which the article can only partly answer, and ask one back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still the person from her option.
run: Ask the two questions for her option, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. Give her time to add the source or to mark her reading.
Then ask her to put one question to you about your own company, and answer it.
exact: Option A, question 1: “When will the route reopen?”
Option A, question 2: “Should we plan for 12-hour shifts too?”
Option B, question 1: “How many people have actually left Norvale?”
Option B, question 2: “Could this happen at our sites?”
Handing the turn over: “Is there anything you want to ask me?”
10.expected: Two answers that say where they come from, and one question from her. Option A, question 1: nobody knows — the carriers expect the route to reopen by the end of the year, and an analyst says it could be March; a complete answer marks both as forecasts, for example “The carriers expect it by the end of the year, but that is a forecast, and one analyst says March.” Question 2 has no answer in the article, so any recommendation marked as hers is correct. Option B, question 1: the article does not know — a union representative says at least 60 since April, so it could be more, and Norvale has not confirmed it. Question 2 is not in the article; any answer marked as her reading is correct. Her question can be as small as “Do you want me to check our own shift plans first?”.
10.support: If she answers without a source, ask “Who says that in the article?” and wait.
10.challenge: Push back once: “So it will be March, then.” Let her answer from the line.
10.monitoring: Whether she marks her reading when the article has no answer, and whether she stays in English when the question is not the one she expected.
10.evidence: Whether she marked her reading without being asked, whether she asked a question of her own, and whether Portuguese appeared.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to run the briefing again for the person from the other option.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write the sentence you noted on screen 9 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. You now play the person from the option she did not choose. She briefs you, starting with what matters most to that person.
exact: Opening the replay, as the CEO: “Just tell me what is certain.”
Opening the replay, as the operations director: “I have to plan next month’s shifts. What do I plan for?”
11.expected: The same article briefed to the other person, with a different point first and the sources kept. A complete second version for the operations director sounds like “What we know for sure is that ships now take nine to twelve days longer and Norvale moved to 12-hour shifts on arrival days. The company says it will hire up to 300 temporary workers, and nobody in the article says it is closing Campinas.” For the CEO, it starts with what is certain and what is only a forecast.
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: Interrupt once more, with a question she has not heard yet, and let her go back to where she was.
11.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the boards appears in the replay.
11.evidence: Whether the point to improve changed in the second version.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you pass on a piece of news, say who says it and whether it has happened or is only expected.”
12.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: reading the article for the story, saying who gives each piece of information, telling what is happening from what is planned and what is possible, keeping up to, at least and between, saying the facts and forecasts with their sources, answering the interruption and going back, and answering the questions after the briefing. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name one sentence she said today with a source and a marker.
12.challenge: Ask where she will use “up to” or “at least” this week.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is a call where a finance director interrupts a presentation with questions nobody prepared.
